questions.explain: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others, leaving delocalised electrons that carry charge.

questions.q: Silicon dioxide is an example of a:
questions.explain: Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure.

questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points?
questions.explain: Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome, not the strong covalent bonds.

questions.q: What happens to particles when a substance boils?
options: They gain energy and spread far apart as a gas
questions.explain: Boiling gives particles enough energy to overcome forces and move freely apart as a gas.

options: Layers of atoms (ions) can slide over each other
questions.explain: Layers of metal ions slide over one another while the metallic bonding holds them together.

questions.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
options: They are made of free electrons
Strong electrostatic forces throughout a giant lattice
questions.explain: Strong electrostatic attractions in the giant ionic lattice need lots of energy to break.

questions.q: Why is diamond unable to conduct electricity?
options: Its layers slide over each other
It has no charged particles free to move
questions.explain: In diamond every electron is held in a covalent bond, so none are free to carry charge.
Electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom, forming ions.
Ionic bonds form when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal.

A single layer of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons
questions.explain: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick, in a hexagonal arrangement.

questions.q: In which state are particles most closely packed and only able to vibrate in fixed positions?
questions.explain: In a solid, particles are tightly packed in a regular arrangement and only vibrate.

questions.q: A covalent bond is formed when atoms:
questions.explain: Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons.
